title: Pooled spatial capture rose from 68% to 71% in a global aftershock test; added location error cut counts after small mainshocks
abstract: We tested whether spatial capture can explain the reported time change in a generic USGS aftershock forecast test. We reused a verified ComCat snapshot and mainshock selection. For 1,415 shallow M6+ mainshocks in 1990-2004 and 1,217 in 2011-2025, we counted M4.6+ events at days 1-30 inside one and two forecast radii. The fraction inside one radius rose from 68.1% to 71.0%. The log10 change was 0.018 (95% mainshock-bootstrap interval -0.063 to 0.083). Equal-sequence weighting and region-magnitude standardization gave similar small changes. The exact periods of the source study also gave small changes at days 1-7, 7-30 and 30-365. In a controlled error experiment, independent Gaussian location error with 10 km standard deviation per coordinate cut recent counts inside one radius by 35% for M6-6.4 mainshocks. This does not measure historical location errors. The data give little support to a change in capture between one and two radii as the main source of the reported calibration shift. They do show that small-mainshock tests are sensitive to location error. Changes beyond both radii, spatially uneven detection and changes in physical sequence geometry remain unresolved.

display.caption: Spatial capture contrasts and the controlled added-error experiment. Error bars are 95% mainshock-bootstrap intervals.
